abstract_snippet: We consider the task of mapping pseudocode to executable code, assuming a one-to-one correspondence between lines of pseudocode and lines of code. Given test cases as a mechanism to validate programs, we search over the space of possible translations of the pseudocode to find a program that compiles and passes the test cases. We collected the SPoC dataset containing 18,356 C++ programs with human-authored pseudocode and test cases. Under a budget of 100 program compilations, performing search improves the synthesis success rate over using the top-one translation from 25.6% to 44.7%.
what_the_paper_supports: SPoC introduces a search-based pseudocode-to-code synthesis pipeline: (1) pseudocode provides line-level specification, (2) code generation model produces candidate translations per line, (3) best-first search with test case validation finds correct programs, (4) error localization (multiclass classifier + prefix-based pruning) identifies failing lines. The SPoC dataset (18,356 C++ programs, 14.7 lines avg, 38.6 test cases avg) is a significant contribution. Test cases serve as executable validation (N7). Compilation serves as a hard gate — 88.7% of failures are compilation errors. Search improves success from 25.6% to 44.7% under 100 compilations.
what_the_paper_does_not_support: No formal specification language beyond pseudocode (GAP-015 — pseudocode is informal). No formal equivalence checking between programs (GAP-017 — only test case validation). No versioning of synthesized programs (GAP-019). No formal verification of program correctness (GAP-020 — only empirical test case checking). No execution trace beyond compilation success/failure (GAP-018 — no intermediate state tracking). Programs limited to C++ with 10-20 lines. One-to-one pseudocode-to-code line assumption is restrictive.
paper_core_claims: Pseudocode-to-code synthesis with search over translation space improves success from 25.6% to 44.7%
Error localization using compiler feedback (88.7% of failures are compilation errors) guides search
Two error localization methods: multiclass classifier (uses error message + pseudocode) and prefix-based pruning (guaranteed correct identification via additional compilations)
SPoC dataset: 18,356 C++ programs with human-authored pseudocode and test cases
Best-first search with credit assignment outperforms naive beam search
Prefix-based pruning is more effective at higher compilation budgets; classifier better at lower budgets

GAP-015.reason: Pseudocode serves as informal line-level specification. Each pseudocode line corresponds to ~1-2 code statements. However, pseudocode is natural language — no formal spec language.

GAP-016.reason: Code generation model compiles pseudocode → code candidates. Search over candidate space with compilation as hard gate. But compilation only checks syntax, not semantics.

GAP-017.reason: Test cases provide behavioral equivalence checking: if program passes all test cases, it's considered correct. But this is testing, not formal equivalence — may miss edge cases.

GAP-018.reason: No intermediate state tracking. Programs are validated only end-to-end via test cases. Error localization identifies failing lines but does not track execution state.

GAP-019.reason: Test cases serve as validation regime, but no versioning or registry of synthesized programs. Search produces a single best program, not a versioned set.

GAP-020.reason: No formal verification. Program correctness is only checked empirically via test cases. No proof of correctness, no edge case coverage guarantee.

N1_FunctionSpec.reason: Pseudocode + test cases as specification. Pseudocode provides line-level guidance, test cases provide functional spec. More structured than I/O-only but still informal.

N2_Representation.reason: Code as representation. Pseudocode-to-code line mapping provides structured decomposition. BPE tokenization for code tokens.

N3_Compiler.reason: Code generation model (BERT-to-BERT style) compiles pseudocode → code candidates. C++ compiler provides hard compilation gate. Two-stage compilation: neural translation + symbolic compilation.

N4_Artifact.reason: Synthesized C++ programs are executable artifacts. SPoC dataset provides reusable artifact collection. But no persistent registry or versioning.

N5_Interpreter.reason: C++ compiler + runtime as interpreter. Test case execution is the validation mechanism. Compilation itself is a hard interpretive gate.

N6_ExecutionTrace.reason: No intermediate execution trace. Error localization identifies failing lines but does not produce execution traces. Only binary success/failure per compilation.

N7_Validator.reason: Test cases as concrete, executable validation. Compilation as syntactic validation. Two-tier validation: (1) does it compile? (2) does it pass test cases? This is a strong, practical validator.

N8_ComposerRouter.reason: Line-by-line composition: each pseudocode line → code line, combined into full program. Search explores different combinations. But composition is sequential, not hierarchical.

N9_VersionedRegistry.reason: No versioning, registry, or retrieval of synthesized programs.

limitations_and_failure_boundaries: One-to-one pseudocode-to-code line assumption — restrictive, doesn't hold for all programs
Only C++ programs, 10-20 lines average — unclear generalization to longer programs or other languages
44.7% success rate means >55% of programs fail even with search
Test case validation is not formal verification — edge cases may be missed
88.7% of failures are compilation errors — semantic errors are harder to catch
Pseudocode quality directly affects synthesis quality — annotator bias possible
No intermediate state tracking — cannot diagnose semantic errors beyond test case failure
strengths_noted: SPoC dataset is a major contribution: 18,356 programs with human-authored pseudocode and test cases
Two error localization methods with complementary strengths (classifier for low budget, prefix pruning for high budget)
Compilation as hard gate is practical and effective — catches 88.7% of failures
Credit assignment via error localization is novel for program synthesis
Dataset and code publicly available: https://sumith1896.github.io/spoc/
Detailed error analysis with prototypical examples (Figure 5)
